title: Why the Richmond sessions are poorly remembered
summary: Surviving players recall little about the Rhythm Kings sessions, and Mares complains jazz writers consult the wrong people.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Can you think, did he ever tell you anything or you of course have done more work probably on research in the New Orleans Rhythm Kings than anyone I know, any details about those sessions that isn't, a lot of that's been written up. Anything that isn't widely known about those sessions? I mean, they were all in Richmond, Indiana, I guess, weren't they? Yeah, that's right. They went over there. Anything about the trips over there that you can remember?

Well, it's a funny thing, Bill, about those things. I spoke to Steve Brown, who made some of those sessions. I talked with Mel Stetzel, who made a lot of them, Georgie Brunas. None of them remember anything vivid. Well, you don't get much detail. No, you can't get details. In fact, Georgie Brunas can't tell you who was on the session. Believe it or not, he can't. If you said, Georgie, who was on this particular tune and so forth, he saw this guy and that guy and he's got them all wrong. Sometimes the piano player changed around a lot. Yeah, they had Kyle and they had Jell-A-Roll, Martin, they had Mel Stetzel, they had Elvis Schoenberg, four or five different piano players played on different records. But they don't remember and I don't know, you get back to those old time musicians and all, you just can't get the thing straightened out. And these jazz books they put out, they all...
And it really gets mixed up. I just thought maybe you might remember certain things that maybe you heard from Paul or other people that you've talked to about these sessions that isn't widely known.

And these jazz book fellows that do this writing for these jazz books, they'll come down here and always contact the wrong people. And if they do, they're going to get the wrong information. And if they run into a certain group, they'll tell them they did everything. They wrote jazz, they made jazz and they did it all, you see. And they really don't get the right story of these things. But I hope it keeps going, Bill.
